description: Maximally structured causal metadata: labels, levels, role, clinical description, physical mechanism, direct parents, direct children, Markov blanket members, CPT shape hints (which parent states most strongly drive each level), and quantitative epidemiological notes where available. Designed to provide the richest possible prior for causal graph recovery.

variables.name: dysp
variables.label: Dyspnoea
variables.description: Shortness of breath; a terminal symptom node in the network.
variables.mechanism: Dyspnoea results from impaired gas exchange or airway obstruction. In this model it is a collider on no path — it is a pure effect node caused by bronchitis (obstructive physiology) and by the 'either' node (TB/cancer parenchymal or mass-effect pathology). Conditioning on dyspnoea activates the explaining-away effect between bronchitis and 'either', creating a spurious dependence between smoking (via bronchitis) and Asia/TB (via either) in the posterior.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(dysp=yes) is highest when both bronc=yes and either=yes (~0.90); elevated when either alone is yes (~0.70) or bronc alone is yes (~0.60); lowest when both are no (~0.10).
variables.quantitative_notes: In the canonical Lauritzen-Spiegelhalter parameterization: P(dysp=yes | either=yes, bronc=yes) ≈ 0.90; P(dysp=yes | either=yes, bronc=no) ≈ 0.70; P(dysp=yes | either=no, bronc=yes) ≈ 0.80; P(dysp=yes | either=no, bronc=no) ≈ 0.10.

variables.name: tub
variables.label: Tuberculosis
variables.description: Pulmonary tuberculosis; an infectious disease node with a geographic risk factor as its sole parent.
variables.mechanism: TB prevalence is substantially higher in many Asian countries than in Western populations; recent travel therefore updates the prior from a background rate of ~0.01 to ~0.05. TB feeds deterministically into the 'either' node. It is d-separated from smoking, bronchitis, and lung cancer given 'either' (or in the absence of conditioning on dyspnoea or xray).
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(tub=yes | asia=yes) ≈ 0.05; P(tub=yes | asia=no) ≈ 0.01. The Asia effect is a ~5-fold relative risk increase.
variables.quantitative_notes: Background TB rate in this model: ~1%. Asia-travel rate: ~1%. Conditional on Asia=yes, TB rate rises to ~5%. These are deliberately unrealistic toy values chosen to make inference tractable; real-world smear-positive TB incidence in high-burden countries is 100–500/100,000/year.

variables.name: lung
variables.label: Lung cancer
variables.description: Primary lung malignancy; caused solely by smoking in this model.
variables.mechanism: Tobacco carcinogens (PAHs, nitrosamines) induce somatic mutations in bronchial epithelium over years of exposure, raising cancer probability roughly 10-fold in smokers vs. non-smokers. Lung cancer shares the 'either' aggregation node with TB, which is why a positive X-ray or dyspnoea cannot distinguish between them. Lung cancer is independent of Asia travel and bronchitis conditional on smoking.
variables.quantitative_notes: Smoker lung cancer rate in model: ~10%. Non-smoker rate: ~1%. Smoking prevalence: ~50%. These toy rates are an order of magnitude higher than realistic lifetime risks to ensure non-trivial posterior probabilities in small samples.

variables.name: bronc
variables.label: Bronchitis
variables.description: Bronchial inflammation; the second smoking-caused disease in the network.
variables.mechanism: Smoking paralyzes mucociliary clearance and directly irritates the bronchial mucosa, producing chronic bronchitis in a large fraction of long-term smokers (~60%). Even in non-smokers a baseline prevalence (~30%) models idiopathic or infectious bronchitis. Bronchitis directly causes dyspnoea and has no path to xray or either, making it informationally isolated from TB and lung cancer except through the collider dyspnoea.
variables.quantitative_notes: Smoking is a common cause of both bronchitis and lung cancer, creating a fork (smoke → bronc, smoke → lung). This is the key latent common cause structure: bronc and lung are marginally dependent but independent given smoke. Conditioning on their shared descendant dyspnoea (via either) re-introduces dependence — the classic Berkson's bias / collider bias pattern.

variables.name: asia
variables.label: Visit to Asia
variables.description: Recent travel to Asia; a root node and sole external risk factor for tuberculosis.
variables.mechanism: Root node with no parents in the model. Encodes epidemiological prior that TB incidence is substantially higher in parts of Asia. Its causal influence is entirely mediated through tuberculosis; it has no direct edges to any other node. Crucially, asia and smoke are marginally independent, and asia and lung/bronc are independent given tub (and absent conditioning on colliders).
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(asia=yes) ≈ 0.01 (marginal prior; rare event in the population).
variables.quantitative_notes: Asia is a low-prevalence root node. Its rarity means it has a weak marginal signal in data, but its conditional effect on TB (5-fold increase) makes it highly informative when TB is observed. This asymmetry — rare cause, large conditional effect — is a common challenge for structure-learning algorithms that rely on marginal association tests.

variables.name: smoke
variables.label: Smoking
variables.description: Tobacco smoking status; the central common cause in the network.
variables.mechanism: Root node with no parents. Smoking is the single most important node in the network from a causal-discovery perspective because it is the common cause (fork) of both lung cancer and bronchitis. Any algorithm that fails to recover smoke as a parent of both will produce a Markov-equivalent but causally incorrect graph. Smoking is marginally independent of Asia, tub, xray, and either in the absence of conditioning on descendants.
variables.quantitative_notes: Smoking prevalence of 50% is intentionally high for a toy model to ensure adequate statistical power for learning both lung and bronc edges. In realistic Western populations prevalence is 15–25%. The high prevalence means the smoke → lung and smoke → bronc edges are among the easiest to recover by any conditional independence test.

variables.name: xray
variables.label: Chest X-ray abnormal
variables.description: Chest radiograph result; a terminal observation node driven exclusively by the 'either' node.
variables.mechanism: X-ray is a noisy, low-specificity test: both TB infiltrates and lung-cancer masses produce similar opacities, so the X-ray result cannot discriminate between them. In this model it has a single parent ('either') and no children, making it a pure measurement leaf. Its high false-positive rate (~5% when either=no) and imperfect sensitivity (~98% when either=yes) model real radiographic uncertainty.
variables.quantitative_notes: The high sensitivity (0.98) but low specificity (1 − 0.05 = 0.95) means that a negative X-ray is strong evidence against TB/cancer, but a positive X-ray is only weakly informative given the low base rates. This models why clinicians cannot diagnose TB or lung cancer from X-ray alone. Conditioning on xray activates explaining-away between tub and lung through the either node — a key inferential pattern in this network.

variables.name: either
variables.label: Tuberculosis or lung cancer present
variables.description: Deterministic logical OR of tuberculosis and lung cancer; an intermediate aggregation node.
variables.mechanism: Encodes the logical disjunction: either=yes if and only if tub=yes or lung=yes (or both). This node is the structural reason that xray and dyspnoea cannot distinguish between TB and lung cancer: both diseases feed into it with equal logical weight. It is a deterministic function of its parents (no noise), so P(either=yes | tub=yes) = 1 and P(either=yes | tub=no, lung=no) = 0. Conditioning on either or its descendants (xray, dysp) creates a v-structure that induces dependence between tub and lung even though they are marginally independent.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: Deterministic OR: P(either=yes | tub=yes, lung=any) = 1; P(either=yes | tub=no, lung=yes) = 1; P(either=yes | tub=no, lung=no) = 0.
variables.quantitative_notes: The deterministic nature of this node creates a hard explaining-away effect: if either=yes is observed and lung=yes is confirmed, then tub becomes less probable (and vice versa). This is the purest example of Berkson's bias in the network. Structure-learning algorithms must correctly identify both tub→either and lung→either edges; failure to do so breaks all downstream inference for xray and dysp. The v-structure (tub → either ← lung) is the single most important v-structure in the Asia network for causal identifiability.
